title: Boolean Gates Extensions
text:
Back-to-Back Cascades: The Non-Commutative Trap
When chaining a logic gate directly into its physical mirror image (its Bayesian inverse), intuition might tempt us to assume that the two transformations always cancel out to form an Identity operator:
\[M \cdot M^{-1} \stackrel{?}{=} I\]
In molecular computing, this naive assumption frequently fails.

Case 1: The 2-Input / 2-Output Cascade (\(\text{And} \cdot \text{And}^{-1} \neq I\))
Here, two input channels (\(A, B\)) are merged through an \(\text{And}\) gate (\(4 \times 2\)), and the resulting single intermediate wire is immediately expanded back through an inverted \(\text{And}^{-1}\) gate (\(2 \times 4\)):

Code
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=12, unit=2.5)

    # 1. Forward AND Gate (pointing right)
    gate_fwd = d.add(logic.And().right().label("And", loc="top"))
    d.add(elm.Line().left(1.5).at(gate_fwd.in1).label("A", loc="left"))
    d.add(elm.Line().left(1.5).at(gate_fwd.in2).label("B", loc="left"))

    # 2. Reverse AND Gate (pointing left, positioned to the right)
    gate_rev = d.add(
        logic.And().left().at((gate_fwd.out[0] + 3.0, gate_fwd.out[1]))
        .label(r"$\text{And}^{-1}$", loc="top")
    )

    # Connecting intermediate wire between the two single pins
    d.add(elm.Line().at(gate_fwd.out).to(gate_rev.out))

    # Output lines emerging on the far right
    d.add(elm.Line().right(1.5).at(gate_rev.in1).label("B'", loc="right"))
    d.add(elm.Line().right(1.5).at(gate_rev.in2).label("A'", loc="right"))












In this configuration, \(\text{And} \cdot \text{And}^{-1}\) does NOT equal the identity (\(I_4\)).

Code
display_inline(r"{And}", r"\cdot", r"{And}^{-1}", "=", (and_q @ and_rev_q).to_katex(show_labels=True))




\[ {And} \cdot {And}^{-1} =  \begin{array}{r|cccc|} \text{} & \text{``00''} & \text{``01''} & \text{``10''} & \text{``11''} \\  \hline \text{``00''} & 0.33 & 0.33 & 0.33 & 0 \\ \text{``01''} & 0.33 & 0.33 & 0.33 & 0 \\ \text{``10''} & 0.33 & 0.33 & 0.33 & 0 \\ \text{``11''} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]





Case 2: The 1-Input / 1-Output Cascade (\(\text{And}^{-1} \cdot \text{And} = I\))
Now, let us reverse the sequence: we begin with a single input channel \(C\), branch it open through an inverted \(\text{And}^{-1}\) gate (\(2 \times 4\)), and immediately recombine the dual branches through a forward \(\text{And}\) gate (\(4 \times 2\)):

Code
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=12, unit=2.5)

    # 1. Reverse AND Gate (expanding 1 wire into 2)
    gate_rev = d.add(logic.And().left().label(r"$\text{And}^{-1}$", loc="top"))
    d.add(elm.Line().left(1.5).at(gate_rev.out).label("C", loc="left"))

    # 2. Forward AND Gate (recombining 2 wires into 1)
    gate_fwd = d.add(
        logic.And().right().at((gate_rev.in1[0] + 3.0, (gate_rev.in1[1] + gate_rev.in2[1]) / 2.0))
        .label("And", loc="top")
    )

    # Connecting the two parallel intermediate lines
    d.add(elm.Line().at(gate_rev.in1).to(gate_fwd.in2))
    d.add(elm.Line().at(gate_rev.in2).to(gate_fwd.in1))

    # Final single output wire on the far right
    d.add(elm.Line().right(1.5).at(gate_fwd.out).label("C'", loc="right"))












In this configuration, \(\text{AND}^{-1} \cdot \text{AND}\) strictly equals the \(2 \times 2\) Identity matrix (\(I_2\))!

Code
display_inline(r"{And}^{-1}", r"\cdot", r"{And}", "=", (and_rev_q @ and_q).to_katex(show_labels=True))




\[ {And}^{-1} \cdot {And} =  \begin{array}{r|cc|} \text{} & \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline \text{``0''} & 1 & 0 \\ \text{``1''} & 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]



Transition matrices can contract or expand the state space dimension, the order of composition strictly dictates whether information is conserved or permanently degraded into probabilistic mixing.

title: Boolean Gates Extensions
section: Random Noise as a Computational Resource
text:
Random Noise as a Computational Resource
In classical digital electronics, randomness is considered an enemy—unwanted thermal noise that must be filtered out. In Conjugated Carbon Computing (CCC), however, stochastic states can be deliberately injected as an active computational resource.
A particularly powerful primitive is the balanced random state (fair coin):

Code
display_inline(r"{Random}", "=", (random).to_katex(show_labels=True))




\[ {Random} =  \begin{array}{r|cc|} \text{} & \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline ~ & 0.5 & 0.5 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]




1. The Random-And Gate
Feeding a balanced random state into one port of an \(\text{And}\) gate suppresses and biases the transmission of signal \(A\):

Code
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=12, unit=2.5)

    gate = d.add(logic.And().right())
    d.add(elm.Line().left(1.8).at(gate.in1).label("A", loc="left"))
    d.add(elm.Line().left(0.5).at(gate.in2).label(r"$\text{Random}$", loc="left"))
    d.add(elm.Line().right(1.5).at(gate.out).label("B", loc="right"))

random_and = ((identity ^ random) @ and_q).normalize()

display_inline(r"\text{Random-And}", "=", r"\Big\{", "(", "Identity", r"\otimes", "Random", ")", r"\cdot", "And", r"\Big\}", "=", random_and.to_katex(show_labels=True))    













\[ \text{Random-And} = \Big\{ ( Identity \otimes Random ) \cdot And \Big\} =  \begin{array}{r|cc|} \text{} & \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline \text{``0''} & 1 & 0 \\ \text{``1''} & 0.5 & 0.5 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]




When \(A = 0\), output \(B\) is deterministically clamped to “0” (\([1 \quad 0]\)).

When \(A = 1\), output \(B\) directly inherits the random distribution \([1/2 \quad 1/2]\).

When one input of a two-input logic gate is held at this balanced stochastic state, the gate ceases to behave like a deterministic switch. Instead, it transforms into a tunable probabilistic filter, modulating the remaining signal \(A\) into output \(B\).


2. The Random-Or Gate
Feeding a balanced random state into an \(\text{Or}\) gate creates a similar dual behavior:

Code
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=12, unit=2.5)

    gate = d.add(logic.Or().right())
    d.add(elm.Line().left(1.8).at(gate.in1).label("A", loc="left"))
    d.add(elm.Line().left(0.5).at(gate.in2).label(r"$\text{Random}$", loc="left"))
    d.add(elm.Line().right(1.5).at(gate.out).label("B", loc="right"))

random_or = ((identity ^ random) @ or_q).normalize()

display_inline(r"\text{Random-Or}", "=", r"\Big\{", "(", "Identity", r"\otimes", "Random", ")", r"\cdot", "Or", r"\Big\}","=", random_or.to_katex(show_labels=True))   













\[ \text{Random-Or} = \Big\{ ( Identity \otimes Random ) \cdot Or \Big\} =  \begin{array}{r|cc|} \text{} & \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline \text{``0''} & 0.5 & 0.5 \\ \text{``1''} & 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]




When \(A = 0\), output \(B\) directly inherits the random distribution \([1/2 \quad 1/2]\).

When \(A = 1\), output \(B\) is deterministically clamped to “1” (\([0 \quad 1]\)).



3. The Random-Xor Gate: The Quantum Jammer / Depolarizer
Feeding a balanced random state into a \(\text{Xor}\) gate produces a striking physical effect:

Code
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=12, unit=2.5)

    gate = d.add(logic.Xor().right())
    d.add(elm.Line().left(1.8).at(gate.in1).label("A", loc="left"))
    d.add(elm.Line().left(0.5).at(gate.in2).label(r"$\text{Random}$", loc="left"))
    d.add(elm.Line().right(1.5).at(gate.out).label("B", loc="right"))

random_xor = ((identity ^ random) @ xor_q).normalize()

display_inline(r"\text{Random-Xor}", "=", r"\Big\{", "(", "Identity", r"\otimes", "Random", ")", r"\cdot", "Xor", r"\Big\}","=", random_xor.to_katex(show_labels=True))     













\[ \text{Random-Xor} = \Big\{ ( Identity \otimes Random ) \cdot Xor \Big\} =  \begin{array}{r|cc|} \text{} & \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline \text{``0''} & 0.5 & 0.5 \\ \text{``1''} & 0.5 & 0.5 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]



Regardless of whether input \(A\) is \(0\) or \(1\), the \(\text{Xor}\) transformation completely scrambles the state.
The Random-Xor gate acts as a perfect hardware depolarizer (entropy injector)—completely erasing the input signal and replacing it with maximal entropy.

title: Boolean Gates Extensions
text:
Partial I/O Inversion (Pin Flipping)
In addition to full forward or backward execution, our molecular architecture permits a far more surgical operation: inverting a single individual input or output pin.
Because a chemical bond is fundamentally an undirected degree of freedom, we can mathematically “fold” a terminal wire backward using our primitive topological operators (such as the Identity, Open, Close, and Bayesian transposition).
This allows us to reconfigure a multi-pin logic component on the fly without resynthesizing the underlying molecular skeleton.

1. Inverting an Input into an Output
Consider a standard 2-input AND gate. What happens if we keep input \(A\) on the left, but rewire the bottom input pin \(B\) so that it folds back and emerges as an output on the right alongside \(C\)?
The component morphs from a 2-in / 1-out gate into a 1-in / 2-out functional beam-splitter:

Code
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=12, unit=2.5)

    # 1. Place the standard AND gate
    and_gate = d.add(logic.And().right())

    # 2. Input A on the left
    d.add(elm.Line().left(2.0).at(and_gate.in1).label("A", loc="left"))

    # 3. Output C on the right
    d.add(elm.Line().right(2.0).at(and_gate.out).label("C", loc="right"))

    # 4. Input B rewired/folded backward into an output pin on the right (B)
    d.add(elm.Line().left(0.8).at(and_gate.in2))
    d.add(elm.Line().down(1.5))
    d.add(elm.Line().right(4.2))
    d.add(elm.Line().right(0.5).label("B", loc="right"))

and1_2 = ((identity ^ open) @ (and_q ^ identity)).normalize()

display_inline(r"\text{And-1-2}", "=", r"\Big\{", "(", "Identity",  r"\otimes", "Open", ")", r"\cdot", "(", "And", r"\otimes",  "Identity", ")", r"\Big\}", "=", and1_2.to_katex(show_labels=True))













\[ \text{And-1-2} = \Big\{ ( Identity \otimes Open ) \cdot ( And \otimes Identity ) \Big\} =  \begin{array}{r|cccc|} \text{} & \text{``00''} & \text{``01''} & \text{``10''} & \text{``11''} \\  \hline \text{``0''} & 0.5 & 0.5 & 0 & 0 \\ \text{``1''} & 0.5 & 0 & 0 & 0.5 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]



In this mode, holding input \(A\) at state "1" forces output \(B\) to match output \(C\) identically, effectively implementing a conditional identity channel.


2. Inverting the Output of an Inverted Gate into an Input
Conversely, consider an inverted gate where an output wire on the right is folded backward to receive signals as an input on the left:

Code
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=12, unit=2.5)

    # 1. Place an inverted AND gate (pointing left)
    and_rev = d.add(logic.And().left())

    # 2. Input C on the far left
    d.add(elm.Line().left(2.0).at(and_rev.out).label("C", loc="left"))

    # 3. Output A on the far right
    d.add(elm.Line().right(2.0).at(and_rev.in2).label("A", loc="right"))

    # 4. Output B folded backward into an input pin on the left (B)
    d.add(elm.Line().right(0.8).at(and_rev.in1))
    d.add(elm.Line().down(1.5))
    d.add(elm.Line().left(4.2))
    d.add(elm.Line().left(0.5).label("B", loc="left"))

and_rev_2_1 = ((and_rev_q ^ identity) @ (identity ^ close)).normalize()

display_inline(r"\text{And-Rev-1-2}", "=", r"\Big\{", "(", r"{And}^{-1}",  r"\otimes", "Identity", ")", r"\cdot", "(", "Identity", r"\otimes",  "Close", ")", r"\Big\}", "=", and_rev_2_1.to_katex(show_labels=True))













\[ \text{And-Rev-1-2} = \Big\{ ( {And}^{-1} \otimes Identity ) \cdot ( Identity \otimes Close ) \Big\} =  \begin{array}{r|cc|} \text{} & \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline \text{``00''} & 0.5 & 0.5 \\ \text{``01''} & 1 & 0 \\ \text{``10''} & 0 & 0 \\ \text{``11''} & 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]





The Power of Topological Rewiring
This partial inversion demonstrates a core principle of Conjugated Carbon Computing: functional directionality is entirely dynamic.

A single physical 3-terminal carbon structure is not permanently etched as a “gate”: it can operate either as a \(2 \rightarrow 1\) logical combiner (forward) or as a \(1 \rightarrow 2\) conditional splitter (partially inverted).

We do not replace physical hardware to change the nature of the operation; we simply reassign which boundary bonds we clamp as inputs and which ones we leave free to oscillate as outputs.

title: Boolean Gates Extensions
section: Correlated Inputs & The Kronecker Product Trap
text:
Correlated Inputs & The Kronecker Product Trap
A common mathematical trap when modeling composite inputs is naively using the Kronecker tensor product (\(A \otimes B\)) when the signals are physically correlated.
Consider a classic test case: a 2-input AND gate where both input pins are tied directly to the very same input wire \(A\) :

Code
with schemdraw.Drawing() as d:
    d.config(fontsize=12, unit=2.5)

    # 1. Place the 2-input AND gate
    and_gate = d.add(logic.And().right())

    # 2. Output wire B
    d.add(elm.Line().right(1.0).at(and_gate.out).label("B", loc="right"))

    # 3. Input wire A branching into both in1 and in2
    in_mid_y = (and_gate.in1[1] + and_gate.in2[1]) / 2.0
    input_A = d.add(elm.Line().right(1.0).at((and_gate.in1[0] - 1.5, in_mid_y)).label("A", loc="left"))
    
    # Route to top input (in1)
    d.add(elm.Wire("-|").at(input_A.end).to(and_gate.in1))

    # Route to bottom input (in2)
    d.add(elm.Wire("-|").at(input_A.end).to(and_gate.in2))













Where the Math Breaks Down
If input \(A\) is a deterministic boolean value ("0" or "1"), no issue arises:
* If \(A = 0\), both pins see \(0\), and the output \(B\) is \(0\).
* If \(A = 1\), both pins see \(1\), and the output \(B\) is \(1\).
The circuit behaves strictly as an Identity buffer (\(B = A\)).
However, watch what happens when input \(A\) carries a probabilistic state (such as our “fair coin” Random bit: \([0.5 \quad 0.5]\)):
If one naively computes the joint input using the tensor product:

Code
random_squared = random ^ random

display_inline("(", "A", r"\otimes", "A", ")", "=", "(", "Random", r"\otimes", "Random", ")", "=", random_squared.to_katex(show_labels=True))




\[ ( A \otimes A ) = ( Random \otimes Random ) =  \begin{array}{r|cccc|} \text{} & \text{``00''} & \text{``01''} & \text{``10''} & \text{``11''} \\  \hline ~ & 0.25 & 0.25 & 0.25 & 0.25 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]



This multiplication fails catastrophically!
The Kronecker product assumes statistical independence: it assigns a \(25\%\) probability to the state "01" and a \(25\%\) probability to "10". But this is a physical impossibility: because both pins are physically wired to the identical bond \(A\), they can never disagree!
The states "01" and "10" make no physical sense on a shared wire.


The Solution: The Split Operator (Coherent Fan-Out)
To duplicate a state while preserving \(100\%\) correlation, we must not compute an independent tensor product. Instead, we must route the single wire through a Split transition matrix:
The Split operator explicitly maps:
* "0" \(\longrightarrow\) "00"
* "1" \(\longrightarrow\) "11"

Code
display_inline("Split", "=", split.to_katex(show_labels=True))




\[ Split =  \begin{array}{r|cccc|} \text{} & \text{``00''} & \text{``01''} & \text{``10''} & \text{``11''} \\  \hline \text{``0''} & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \text{``1''} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]



When input \(A\) passes through the Split matrix, it produces the true correlated joint state:

Code
display_inline("A", r"\cdot", "Split", "=", (random @ split).to_katex(show_labels=True))




\[ A \cdot Split =  \begin{array}{r|cccc|} \text{} & \text{``00''} & \text{``01''} & \text{``10''} & \text{``11''} \\  \hline ~ & 0.5 & 0 & 0 & 0.5 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]



Now, cascading this properly into the AND gate restores mathematical and physical truth:

Code
display_inline("(", "A", r"\cdot", "Split", ")", r"\cdot", "And", "=", "B")

display_inline((random @ split).to_katex(), r"\cdot", and_q.to_katex(), "=", ((random @ split) @ and_q).to_katex(), "=", "A")




\[ ( A \cdot Split ) \cdot And = B \]




\[  \begin{array}{|cccc|}  \hline 0.5 & 0 & 0 & 0.5 \\  \hline \end{array}  \cdot  \begin{array}{|cc|}  \hline 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array}  =  \begin{array}{|cc|}  \hline 0.5 & 0.5 \\  \hline \end{array}  = A \]



The identity \(B = A\) is preserved, the impossible states are purged, and the correlation is maintained with mathematical perfection.

However, this breakthrough carries a profound theoretical consequence: deterministic certainty dissolves here.
Because a single input state maps to multiple admissible physical configurations, classical boolean determinism can no longer describe the computation. We are inevitably forced to expand our mathematical framework into the domain of statistics.

title: Quantum Chemistry Part 2
text:
Probabilistic Bits (p-bits)
Probabilistic bits provide a robust mathematical framework for encoding and processing information. By applying this formalism to carbon-carbon bonds, we can natively capture the stochastic nature of chemical systems and open up new frontiers in molecular computing.
Think of a coin toss. Once flipped, the coin can land on tails (state “0”) or heads (state “1”).
With a fair coin, there is an equal probability — a 50% chance—of landing on state “0” and a 50% chance of landing on state “1”.
Mathematically, we formulate probabilistic bits using the same transition matrices introduced earlier. The only operational difference lies in the continuous values of the matrix elements rather than discrete binary indicators.

A fair coin:



Code
display_inline("Fair", "=", random.to_katex(show_labels=True))


\[ Fair =  \begin{array}{r|cc|} \text{} & \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline ~ & 0.5 & 0.5 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]


The first element quantifies the probability of observing a “0”; the second element quantifies the probability of observing a “1”.
We could also bias the coin so that it carries a one-in-four chance (25%) of landing on “0”, and a three-in-four chance (75%) of landing on “1”.

A biased coin:



Code
biased = TransitionMatrix([
    [0.25, 0.75]
])

display_inline("Biased", "=", biased.to_katex(show_labels=True))


\[ Biased =  \begin{array}{r|cc|} \text{} & \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline ~ & 0.25 & 0.75 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]


The limiting boundary case occurs when there is a 0% chance of being in one state and a 100% chance of being in the other. Under these conditions, deterministic certainty is recovered, and the probabilistic bit collapses back into a classical boolean bit (\([1, 0]\) or \([0, 1]\)).
Any transition matrix is physically and computationally admissible in our model if it satisfies three structural properties:

Bounded Probabilities: Every individual element must lie strictly within the closed interval \([0, 1]\) (no negative or super-unitary probabilities).

Conservation of Probability: For any accessible state, the elements along the row must sum to exactly 1 (100% of the probability distribution, ensuring no leakage into unmodeled states).

Forbidden Inputs: If an input configuration is topologically or chemically forbidden by the molecular network, all elements along that row sum to exactly 0, acting as an algebraic filter that rejects unphysical states.


We can now derive the complete transition matrix for the Double Honeycomb molecule (with bond 𝐴 as an input and bond 𝐵 as an output):

Code
doubleHoneycomb = TransitionMatrix.from_resonances(all_resonances)

display_inline("DoubleHoneycomb", "=", doubleHoneycomb.to_katex(show_labels=True))




\[ DoubleHoneycomb =  \begin{array}{r|cc|} \text{} & \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline \text{``0''} & 0.5 & 0.5 \\ \text{``1''} & 1 & 0 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]



Examining the matrix reveals an interesting hybrid behavior:
* When input \(A\) is held at “0”, output \(B\) behaves as a fair coin (\([0.5 \quad 0.5]\)), exhibiting true probabilistic branching.
* When input \(A\) is held at “1”, output \(B\) collapses into a deterministic boolean bit strictly clamped to “0” (\([1.0 \quad 0.0]\)).

The universal logic deadlock is officially broken. We now possess a tangible molecular blueprint for universal boolean computation etched directly into a conjugated carbon skeleton.

title: Quantum Chemistry Part 2
text:
Dual-Rail Interconnects
Now that we have successfully synthesized a universal NOR gate within a closed-form molecule, a critical architectural question emerges: how do we chain these logic gates together to build complex circuits?
The naive approach—connecting functional blocks via a single, isolated carbon bond as we did with elementary junctions—is no longer viable.
Examine what happens when we open one of the inputs of our “Letter Envelope” molecule: it does not terminate in a single dangling bond, but rather in a symmetric pair of coupled branches. Due to the internal geometry of the resonance network, these two parallel branches are physically locked together—they will always carry the exact same logical state simultaneously.

Code
# Create a conjugated carbon molecule
mol = CarbonMolecule("Letter Envelope")

# Add atoms

title: Qubit Emulation
text:
Representing a Qubit with Protobits
On the surface, qubits and protobits appear fundamentally incompatible:

Qubits are described by state vectors with negative and complex probability amplitudes (\(\mathbb{C}^2\)). This complex phase allows wavefunctions to interfere constructively or destructively (adding or subtracting amplitudes).

Protobits, operating within stochastic transition matrices, are defined purely over real, non-negative probabilities (\(p \in [0, 1]\)), with no native complex phase.

Yet, we have already proven that the molecular gates achieve universal computation. Any mathematical operation—including complex arithmetic and phase rotations—can be synthesized algebraically.
All that is required now is the optimal geometric mapping.

Deconstructing the Bloch Sphere
Geometrically, a single qubit lives on the continuous surface of a three-dimensional unit sphere: the Bloch Sphere.
To reconstruct the full expressive richness of a spherical state space using only positive-probability protobits, linear algebra dictates that we need a minimum of three independent dimensions.
To completely define the state of a qubit without invoking imaginary numbers in the underlying hardware, we decompose the state across three distinct functional protobits:

The Presence Protobit (\(A_2\)):
Encodes the vertical projection (along the \(Z\)-axis), determining whether the measurement collapses toward \(|0\rangle\) or \(|1\rangle\).

The Imaginary Phase Protobit (\(A_1\)):
Governs circular phase along the \(Y\)-axis, encoding the imaginary depth of the quantum state (\(+1\) or \(+i\)).

The Sign Phase Protobit (\(A_0\)):
Governs real interference along the \(X\)-axis, determining whether wave amplitudes add constructively (\(+1\)) or destructively (\(-1\)).




The 8 Extremal Basis States
When these three protobits are combined through the Kronecker product, they span an 8-dimensional configuration space (\(2^3 = 8\)).
These 8 discrete basis states map directly to the 8 vertices of a state cube, perfectly capturing the cardinal projections along with their fundamental discrete phase orientations (\(\pm 1, \pm i\)):
\[\text{``000''} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow |0\rangle\]
\[\text{``001''} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow -|0\rangle\]
\[\text{``010''} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} i \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow i|0\rangle\]
\[\text{``011''} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} -i \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow -i|0\rangle\]
\[\text{``100''} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow |1\rangle\]
\[\text{``101''} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow -|1\rangle\]
\[\text{``110''} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ i \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow i|1\rangle\]
\[\text{``111''} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -i \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow -i|1\rangle\]
By taking convex linear combinations (superpositions) across these 8 positive protobit states, we can reconstruct any arbitrary point \((\theta, \phi)\) on the Bloch sphere.
The mystery of complex quantum phases dissolves into real, positive geometry. Three simple carbon bonds are all that nature needs to house a complete quantum qubit.

section: Quantum Logic Gates as Cube Rotations
text:
Quantum Logic Gates as Cube Rotations
Implementing the continuous rotation of a quantum logic gate might appear daunting at first glance. In our discrete framework, however, the problem simplifies drastically: all we need to specify is where the 8 vertices of our state cube map to.
Think of tracking an airplane flying across a pitch-black night sky:
Inside the cockpit, the pilot relies on continuous gyroscopes and altitude instruments. But an observer standing on the ground below cannot see the fuselage of the plane at all. All they can see are the plane’s exterior navigation lights:
* A red light on the left wingtip,
* A green light on the right wingtip,
* A white beacon on the tail / belly.
Even though the observer only tracks three discrete points of light, they can unambiguously deduce the airplane’s full three-dimensional spatial orientation.
If the observer initially sees the red light on the left, the green light on the right, and the white beacon underneath—and a moment later observes the red light on the right, the green light on the left, and the white beacon on top—they know with absolute mathematical certainty that the aircraft has executed a \(180^\circ\) roll.
We treat quantum logic gates in precisely the same way:
We do not need to model an intractable, continuous spherical rotation across the entire continuum of the Bloch sphere. We simply track the permutation of our 8 discrete basis vertices.
By tracking how these extremal “navigation lights” permute across our protobit coordinates, the global unitary transformation naturally takes care of itself.

title: Qubit Emulation
text:
Elementary Single-Qubit Gates
The standard Pauli gates—\(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\), along with the phase gate \(S\)—are classified as “simple” in our framework for two structural reasons:
1. They operate strictly on a single logical qubit (one 3-protobit channel in, one 3-protobit channel out).
2. Every vertex of our 8-state cube maps cleanly and deterministically onto another exact vertex of the cube. There is no splitting of amplitudes or fractional dispersion across vertices.
Consequently, in this discrete representation, implementing a quantum gate reduces fundamentally to implementing a truth table permutation.
Keep in mind that while these circuits are structurally composed of boolean logic components, they operate as quantum transition operators capable of manipulating protobit states. We established their mathematical foundation earlier in “A Refresher on Boolean Logic” and “Boolean Gates Extensions” using transition matrix formalism.


The X Gate (Pauli-X / Bit-Flip)
The \(X\) operator swaps the basis states \(|0\rangle \leftrightarrow |1\rangle\). It corresponds to a \(\pi\) (\(180^\circ\)) rotation around the \(X\)-axis of the Bloch sphere:
\[X = |1\rangle\langle 0| + |0\rangle\langle 1| = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

The Universe as a Clifford Algebra of Protobits

Decomposing a qubit reveals a profound mathematical bridge: it takes \((m + n)\) protobits to span the \(2^{m+n}\) multivector space of a Geometric Clifford Algebra \(\mathcal{C}\ell(m, n)\).

Continuous complex numbers and ethereal wavefunctions are merely emergent illusions. Reality does not compute with abstract qubits in unphysical Hilbert spaces—it weaves the grammar of \(\mathcal{C}\ell(m, n)\) through the physical resonance of Protobits.

Parallels with the I Ching

The 64 Hexagrams (\(2^6\)) naturally map to a 2-qubit interacting register!

Visually and geometrically, the natural hexagonal tiling of a turtle shell bears an uncanny resemblance to the fused aromatic rings and polygonal lattices of our molecular carbon logic gates.

The King Wen Sequence: When mapped as a discrete state transition matrix, the traditional King Wen permutation order exhibits the algebraic properties of a unitary, reversible 2-input / 2-output Universal quantum gate.

I will certainly not claim that ancient diviners possessed an explicit formulation of quantum mechanics; there is zero historical evidence for such an assertion.
However, it is deeply fascinating to realize that our modern concepts of superposition, dual-rail binary states, and molecular resonance would have felt astonishingly familiar to their worldview.
Perhaps when humans search for the fundamental patterns of change in nature, all roads eventually lead back to the same underlying geometric syntax.

Common Objections

“A molecule featuring a three-membered ring would be energetically unstable due to extreme ring strain.”

Quite right! If you ever read a headline announcing that a chemist has isolated a naked, three-membered conjugated carbon ring folded into an “envelope,” it would be nothing short of a miracle. The angle strain alone would tear it apart under ambient conditions.
The molecular graphs presented here are functional topologies — logical schematics rather than literal chemical blueprints.
However, remember our golden rule of interconnects: inserting an even number of carbon atoms into any bond preserves the exact logical identity of the circuit.
As a practical rule of thumb in molecular architecture: if a topology suffers from geometric strain or a lack of space, expand it by inserting pairs of carbon atoms.
By doing so, the bond angles relax toward the natural \(120^\circ\) planar geometry of stable \(sp^2\) carbon. What begins as an overly strained toy graph eventually transitions into a thermodynamically stable, synthesizable molecule at ambient temperature and pressure.
Take our strained “Letter Envelope” model as a prime example:

Pyracylene is not a theoretical fantasy: it is a real, well-documented molecule synthesized in organic chemistry laboratories (and famously observed as dynamic defects in graphene sheets under electron-beam irradiation).
It must be noted, however, that pyracylene has often been characterized by physical chemists as “borderline aromatic” (owing to the delicate balance between its aromatic benzene-like cores and its antiaromatic cyclooctatetraene-like peripheries).
Which brings us directly to the next objection…


“Several of these proposed topologies are non-aromatic, meaning their resonance structures are by no means equiprobable.”

This is a profound physical objection grounded in Hückel’s Rule of Aromaticity.
In physical chemistry, a planar, cyclic conjugated ring is exceptionally stable (aromatic) if it possesses \((4n + 2)\) delocalized \(\pi\)-electrons (such as the 6 \(\pi\)-electrons in benzene).
Conversely, when a ring contains \(4n\) \(\pi\)-electrons (like cyclooctatetraene with 8 electrons), it enters an antiaromatic, electronically frustrated regime. To escape this high-energy penalty, the molecule undergoes a conformational distortion: it buckles out of the plane, warping into a non-planar geometry — much like a potato chip or a saddle.
Once planarity is broken:
* The overlap between adjacent \(p_z\) atomic orbitals collapses.
* The continuous \(\pi\)-cloud fragments into localized, unequal bond lengths.
* The resonance states split into widely different energy levels, destroying the uniform probabilistic branching required for clean logic transitions.
Constraining computational designs strictly to Hückel-compliant \((4n + 2)\) rings would tend to cripple our architectures. Efficient logic circuits inevitably demand topologies that violate standard aromatic electron counts.
How do we overcome this energetic divergence? By enforcing planarity through mechanical tension.
If non-aromatic rings buckle because of electronic strain, we can physically prevent that distortion by anchoring the molecule within an external structural scaffold and adjusting its perimeter tension — much like stretching and tuning a drumhead.
When clamped flat by external mechanical boundaries:
1. Out-of-plane buckling modes are geometrically suppressed.
2. Orbital overlap is uniformly restored across all carbon vertices.
3. The competing resonance configurations are forced into equipotential energy levels.
Several realistic nanotechnology platforms could serve as this planarizing frame:

Perforated Graphene Frameworks: A pristine monolayer graphene sheet on a support can be nanolithographically patterned with nanopores. Molecular logic units can then be suspended across these nanometer-scale voids, anchored at the edges using natural heteroatomic “clips” — specifically divalent oxygen bridges (\(C-O-C\), ether linkages) or trivalent nitrogen junctions (\(C-N-C_2\), tertiary amine nodes) standard in organic synthesis.

Protein and Enzyme Scaffolds: In biological systems, enzymes frequently force substrate molecules into chemically unnatural, high-energy planar transition states through rigid hydrophobic binding pockets. Supramolecular protein cages could act as macroscopic templates, mechanically clamping carbon logic circuits into the required planar topology.

Atomically Flat Substrates (On-Surface Template Synthesis): A proven technique in modern molecular electronics consists of depositing molecular precursors onto ultra-flat crystalline surfaces—such as gold \(Au(111)\) or thin insulating layers of sodium chloride (\(NaCl\)) on copper. Strong interfacial van der Waals forces act as an electrostatic press, physically flattening the carbon backbone against the substrate and completely quenching out-of-plane buckling modes.
Covalent Organic Frameworks (COFs): Rather than manually carving cavities into existing materials, one can synthesize self-assembling 2D crystalline polymer sheets known as COFs. These frameworks naturally form rigid, highly ordered porous networks. Molecular logic units can be engineered as modular tiles that integrate seamlessly into the lattice pores, leveraging the surrounding network as a built-in, thermally stable rigid chassis.
Nanotube Suspension Tensors: Suspending the molecular network between parallel single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) allows for active, dynamic mechanical tuning. By applying controlled electrostatic fields or piezo-actuation across the nanotube anchors, the external tension on the circuit can be adjusted in real time—the nanomechanical equivalent of tuning pegs on a guitar.

Admittedly, experimental optimal scaffolding techniques remains an open frontier. What matters at this stage is that viable physical pathways exist: there are no thermodynamics violation; we simply need to engineer the boundary constraints.


“Larger molecular networks would suffer from rapid environmental decoherence in any realistic, noisy medium.”

There is indeed a fundamental spatial threshold — a coherence length — beyond which fragile quantum entanglement decays into classical noise.
Crucially, this coherence length is not a fixed, rigid constant: it is heavily dictated by thermal thermodynamics.
While cooling the system down to cryogenic temperatures (\(4\ \text{K}\) or millikelvin regimes) would trivially expand the coherence horizon across tens of micrometers — instantly covering millions of interconnected gates — our core design philosophy refuses the crutch of bulky, energy-expensive dilution refrigerators. The ultimate objective remains robust, room-temperature operation.
In such environments, noise originates primarily from two physical culprits:
1. Lattice Vibrations (Phonons): Thermal agitations cause the carbon-carbon bonds to flex, stretch, and twist at picosecond timescales (\(10^{-12}\ \text{s}\)), disrupting the delicate phase relationships of the delocalized \(\pi\)-electron wavefunctions.
2. Magnetic Spin Fluctuations: Uncontrolled nuclear spins (such as trace \(^{13}\text{C}\) isotopes or surrounding solvent protons) generate fluctuating local magnetic fields that dephase electron spins.
In pristine conjugated materials (such as graphene or polyenes) at room temperature, the electron mean free path and ballistic quantum coherence radius typically span from tens to hundreds of nanometers (roughly 50 to 500 carbon rings). Across a macroscopic chip, this boundary would inevitably be crossed.
But here lies the remarkable resilience of molecular architectures: decoherence does not kill the machine.
As long as the molecular network remains electrically insulated from parasitic ground leaks, it does not catastrophically shut down when quantum coherence is lost. Instead, it undergoes graceful degradation, seamlessly transitioning from coherent quantum computing into massively parallel probabilistic computing.
While a probabilistic p-bit network lacks the exponential speedup of pure quantum computation, it remains a formidable thermodynamic supercomputer — capable of solving problems at the sub-picosecond physical timescale of electron motion, while operating near the fundamental thermodynamic limits of minimal energy dissipation.
Note however that in any realistic large-scale molecular circuit, computation inherently operates across two spatial tiers:
* Local Scale (Quantum Islands): Within individual logic gates, rings, and tightly coupled blocks (spanning a few nanometers), operation is 100% coherent and quantum.
* Global Scale: Between distant sub-units separated by long interconnects, the signal propagates as incoherent, probabilistic bitstreams.
So now the ultimate architectural challenge is straightforward: how do we expand the quantum islands until they engulf the entire circuit?
Several physical mechanisms can push the coherence horizon across the entire network:

Topological Protection & Chiral Edge Modes (Quantum Hall Analogs): By engineering the graph topology to mimic the Haldane model or quantum spin Hall phases, conduction electrons are confined to robust, unidirectional edge states. In these topological conduits, back-scattering against thermal phonons is physically forbidden, dramatically stretching the coherence length across macroscopic boundaries.

Passive Stabilizer Couplers (Noiseless Subsystems): Our inter-branch couplers act as hardware-level, passive quantum error-correcting codes. By enforcing mutual parity between dual-rail lines through electrostatic and quantum exchange energy, the coupler creates an energetic penalty against phase-flip and bit-flip errors. Noise that attempts to perturb a single branch is energetically suppressed, confining quantum information inside an intrinsically protected noiseless subsystem (decoupling subspace) without requiring active error-detection cycles.

Isotopic Purification: Synthesizing the carbon framework from \(99.99\%\) isotopically pure Carbon-12 completely eradicates the nuclear spin bath. The \(\pi\)-electrons travel through a magnetically silent vacuum, extending room-temperature spin coherence by orders of magnitude.

Phononic Bandgap Engineering: Designing the surrounding scaffolding (such as periodic perforated graphene or COFs) as an acoustic metamaterial creates a phononic bandgap. By acoustically isolating the molecular circuit, the specific vibrational frequencies responsible for thermal dephasing are physically barred from penetrating the computational core.

Ultrafast Femtosecond Dynamics: Molecular \(\pi\)-electron resonance and charge redistribution occur on the femtosecond scale (\(10^{-15}\ \text{s}\)), completing logical transitions orders of magnitude faster than the picosecond onset of thermal lattice vibrations. The computation finishes before the environment even notices it has begun.



“How are the physical inputs and outputs concretely interfaced with the rest of the circuit?”

This is the classic “interconnect problem.” A computational model is useless if it remains trapped in an isolated mathematical vacuum. We must be able to write an input state into a carbon bond and read the output state from another bond.
Fortunately, we do not need to invent new physics to interface with carbon bonds. Modern nanotechnology and physical chemistry already offer an exhaustive toolkit, which can be grouped into five distinct physical categories:

1. Mechanical Methods (Strain & Geometry)
The bond state is dictated by physically tuning atomic distances (\(1.54\ \text{Å}\) for single bonds vs \(1.34\ \text{Å}\) for double bonds).
* Writing (Inputs): Nanoscale piezoelectric actuators or Atomic Force Microscope (AFM) tips can gently stretch or compress boundary bonds, mechanically clamping them into an elongated single bond (\(0\)) or a contracted double bond (\(1\)).
* Reading (Outputs): Non-contact AFM (NC-AFM with a CO-functionalized tip) can directly “feel” and image the electronic bond order of terminal bonds with sub-angstrom resolution.


2. Chemical & Electrochemical Methods (Bond Valency)
The bond state is controlled by reversibly adding or removing atoms and electrons.
* Writing (Inputs): Reversible protonation (attaching a single hydrogen ion \(H^+\)) saturates an input carbon atom into a four-way \(\sigma\)-node, permanently locking the adjacent conjugated pathway into a single bond (\(0\)). Removing the proton frees the \(\pi\)-electron, restoring the double-bond state (\(1\)).
* Reading (Outputs): Double bonds are chemically far more reactive than single bonds (e.g., in cycloaddition reactions). The output state can trigger or inhibit a localized chemical cascade.


3. Electrostatic & Inductive Methods (Contact-Free Fields)
Information is transferred across the vacuum using local electric fields (Stark effect) and our Couplers.
* Writing (Inputs): A metallic nano-gate positioned a single nanometer away applies a local voltage bias. The electrostatic field polarizes the \(\pi\)-electron cloud, pushing double-bond density into the target bond without any physical contact.
* Reading (Outputs): A Single-Electron Transistor (SET) or capacitive sensor placed beside the terminal bond detects the minute electrostatic charge shift caused by single vs double bond transitions.


4. Optical & Photonic Methods (Speed of Light)
Photons drive transitions and read results non-destructively.
* Writing (Inputs): Molecular photoswitches (such as azobenzene or diarylethene units) bonded to the input lines can be flipped between two conformations using specific wavelengths of light (UV vs visible laser pulses), injecting a \(0\) or \(1\) in femtoseconds.
* Reading (Outputs): Fluorescence spectroscopy. When the output circuit resolves to a continuous conjugated path (\(1\)), it fluoresces brightly under laser excitation; if the path is broken into single bonds (\(0\)), fluorescence is quenched. The output bit is read out with an ordinary photodetector.


5. Magnetic & Spintronic Methods (The \(^{13}\text{C}\) Nuclear Bridge)
Leveraging magnetic resonance and nuclear spins for ultra-stable read/write operations.
* Writing (Inputs): Radiofrequency (RF) pulses flip a designated terminal \(^{13}\text{C}\) nuclear spin, which then imprints its logical state onto the surrounding \(\pi\)-electrons via hyperfine contact.
* Reading (Outputs): Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) diamond magnetometers can optically detect the nanoscale magnetic signature of the output bond state non-invasively at room temperature.


Summary: Matching the Interface to the Architecture
We do not have to rely on a single interface. The physical mechanism can be chosen to fit the exact purpose of the machine:

Plants lack a nervous system, yet the sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica) can learn to ignore harmless falls and retain that memory for weeks. Trees synchronize resource distribution across vast fungal networks and anticipate daily solar cycles long before dawn. Rather than relying on fragile electrical action potentials, plants may process and store environmental information directly within their rich architecture of aromatic compounds and carbon lattices. Life spent nearly four billion years computing with carbon bonds before it ever evolved a brain. Neurons might be high-speed cables connecting nature’s ancient, organic computers.

section: Mapping a Continuous Qubit into a 3-Protobit State Vector
text:
Mapping a Continuous Qubit into a 3-Protobit State Vector
How do we take an arbitrary, continuous quantum qubit state \(|\psi\rangle\) defined over complex numbers and convert it into our discrete, strictly non-negative \(1 \times 8\) protobit transition matrix?
A general qubit state is written in Dirac notation as:
\[|\psi\rangle = c_0 |0\rangle + c_1 |1\rangle = \begin{bmatrix} c_0 \\ c_1 \end{bmatrix}\]
where \(c_0, c_1 \in \mathbb{C}\) are complex probability amplitudes.
We can expand each complex coefficient into its real and imaginary parts:
\[c_0 = \text{Re}(c_0) + i \, \text{Im}(c_0)\] \[c_1 = \text{Re}(c_1) + i \, \text{Im}(c_1)\]
This gives us 4 real numbers: \(\text{Re}(c_0), \, \text{Im}(c_0), \, \text{Re}(c_1), \, \text{Im}(c_1)\).
However, these real numbers can be negative, whereas our protobit transition matrices require strictly non-negative probabilities (\(p \ge 0\)).
To eliminate negative numbers without losing any phase information, we decompose every real value \(x\) into its positive component (\(x^+\)) and negative component (\(x^-\)):
\[x = x^+ - x^- \quad \text{where} \quad x^+ = \max(x, 0), \quad x^- = \max(-x, 0)\]
Notice that \(x^+\) and \(x^-\) are both non-negative (\(\ge 0\)), and at least one of them is always zero!
Applying this split to our 4 real parameters yields exactly 8 non-negative values (\(p_0\) through \(p_7\)):
\[p_0 = \max({Re}(c_0), 0)\] \[p_1 = \max({-Re}(c_0), 0)\] \[p_2 = \max({Im}(c_0), 0)\] \[p_3 = \max({-Im}(c_0), 0)\] \[p_4 = \max({Re}(c_1), 0)\] \[p_5 = \max({-Re}(c_1), 0)\] \[p_6 = \max({Im}(c_1), 0)\] \[p_7 = \max({-Im}(c_1), 0)\]
To satisfy the conservation of probability, where all row elements must sum to \(1.0\), we compute the \(L_1\)-norm scalar:
\[S = \sum_{k=0}^{7} p_k\]
Finally, we normalize each component:
\[\mathbf{P} = \frac{1}{S} \begin{bmatrix} p_0 & p_1 & p_2 & p_3 & p_4 & p_5 & p_6 & p_7 \end{bmatrix}\]
The resulting \(1 \times 8\) row vector \(\mathbf{P}\) is a valid, normalized, non-negative probability distribution over our 3 protobits.
Not a single bit of information, amplitude, or complex phase from the original qubit is lost. It has simply been unpacked into an 8-channel stochastic representation!
